title: Benchmarking with a workload that reproduces the real one

videos.script: A benchmark is a promise about the future. It says: this server, with this change, will handle the traffic you have. {{promise}} Most benchmarks break that promise before the first run. They measure somebody else's traffic, for ten seconds, on a cache that was already warm. {{break}} PostgreSQL ships a benchmark of its own, pgbench, and its built-in test is a bank from the nineteen nineties. Four tables, all writes, nothing like a marketplace. {{bank}} Its number is real. It is just not about you. {{notyou}} In this lesson you turn pgbench into a copy of your own traffic. The scripts come from lesson 2. The weights come from what pg_stat_statements counted, not from a guess. {{weights}} Then you read a report properly: throughput, average latency, the spread around it, and the latency of every statement in every script. {{report}} You walk into the traps on purpose. A run that is too short. A cache that is cold. A client stealing processor time from the server it is measuring. {{traps}} And you run the same benchmark several times, because one run is an anecdote. The spread between runs is the size of the smallest change you can believe. {{repeat}}
